glibc_daemon_and_kernel_on_linux.evidence: Direction D1 has its own CI-produced record (evidence/20261031-d1-glibc-arm64.json): the daemon built against glibc passed the runtime contract, the E3 hardening suite and C-vs-Rust parity on an ubuntu-24.04-arm runner, and the released static kernel booted a guest there which reported aarch64 and its own release from inside the guest.

panel_shows_real_daemon_state.evidence: tests/test-panel.sh: 13 assertion(s) passed, 0 failed. It runs a real daemon in selftest mode, writes the registry record the launcher owns, starts the panel against it and asserts the reply; node then executes the page's own script (panel/render-check.mjs) against that live reply and asserts the nodes it created, because this device has no browser engine (Playwright: "Unsupported platform: android"). State is read through protocol v1 (status, ports), never from daemon files; the page is read-only and loopback-only by design.

recipes_measured_on_device.evidence: bench/recipes.sh drove real workloads through a live guest: 10x "docker run --rm alpine true" with a warm image took 157404 ms in total (15740 ms median per container start; the alpine image occupies 8657121 bytes); nginx in one container served 500 requests at concurrency 10 to ab in another container at 76.32 req/s (131.023 ms per request). Local registry (push + pull of a built image): NO NUMBER, and the reason is now known rather than guessed. The recipe itself is blocked before it starts: pulling registry:2 from Docker Hub inside the guest did not complete in over ten minutes on this device, while smaller images (alpine, nginx:alpine, httpd:alpine) pulled and ran fine in the same guest, so it is image size over the guest network and not a broken path. What was verified is the mechanism: the recipe script was uploaded in four base64 chunks over the exec channel and the guest executed it, printing its own R3F...-START and R3F...-S1 markers -- which is what proved the exec channel silently drops a command line above roughly 568 bytes (569 bytes arrived, 2182 bytes did nothing at all with rc=0) and is why bench/guest-put.sh exists.

boot.evidence: A guest booted twice in this direction: on the glibc aarch64 runner (D1, evidence/20261031-d1-glibc-arm64.json, verified from inside the guest) and on this device, where bench/recipes.sh drove containers through a live guest running dockerd.

exec_channel_line_limit.evidence: Measured on the device: a 569-byte exec command reached the guest intact, a 2182-byte one produced no guest output at all while the daemon reported success. The guest agent reads one line from /dev/console and evals it, and the PTY line discipline truncates beyond that. Documented in docs/RUNTIME-CONTRACT.md 9a together with the two rules it implies (chunk long scripts; keep markers base64 so the console echo cannot satisfy an assertion).

known_limits_observed: no browser engine on this device, so the panel is verified by executing its script in node rather than by rendering it in a browser
the container-start number includes UML itself: it is what a user waits for, and it is tens of seconds, not fractions of one
the exec channel delivers one console line, and a line above ~568 bytes is dropped in silence (the client sees rc=0), so long scripts must be uploaded in chunks
registry:2 could not be pulled inside the guest within ten minutes, so the local-registry recipe has no number on this device
